title: From Plastic Bottle to Cookie: Scientists Engineer Yeast to Make Food from Waste
summary:
Imagine biting into a cookie made from a plastic bottle. It sounds impossible, but scientists at Southern Illinois University Carbondale are turning that idea into a real project. They have engineered yeast — tiny living organisms used in baking — to convert plastic and plant waste into edible proteins, vitamins, and flavorings.

The process starts with polyethylene terephthalate (PET), the plastic used in soda and water bottles. PET is full of carbon. So are corn stalks and leaves left over from farms. The researchers use a technique called oxidative hydrothermal dissolution, which combines water and oxygen at high heat and pressure to break these tough materials into smaller molecules. Then they feed those molecules to specially programmed yeast, including baker's yeast. The yeast acts like a tiny factory, transforming the molecules into proteins, fats, and acids.

Once the yeast has done its job, the scientists mix the results with fiber, starch, and sweetener. That mixture goes through a 3D printer to create protein-rich cookies called µBites (pronounced "microbites").

The project grew out of a NASA-led effort to produce food in deep space, where astronauts cannot rely on regular shipments from Earth. "We were trying to develop technologies for plastic upcycling to make more valuable products," says Associate Professor Lahiru Jayakody. "We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon."

Jayakody adds, "Microbes are very clever. So, we are using their traits to solve the problems we created." The team says available data show µBites are safe to eat, but they are still waiting for institutional approval before holding formal taste tests. If successful, the technology could help feed people in disaster zones or on long space missions — turning trash into dinner.
why_it_matters: The plastic bottle that goes into a school recycling bin is usually the end of the story, but this project suggests it could be the beginning of one — if the food it produces is proven safe and regulators allow it, today's teenagers may grow up in a world where 'waste' and 'food' are not always opposites.

background_read: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is one of the most common plastics on Earth, used in drink bottles, and because it is cheap and strong, huge amounts of it end up as litter instead of being recycled.

Southern Illinois University Carbondale, the public university in the U.S. state of Illinois where this yeast work is happening, is one of the teams that took part in NASA's Deep Space Food Challenge — a competition asking researchers to design food systems astronauts could use where no supply ships can reach them.
Lahiru Jayakody (the associate professor who leads the project) points out that plastic and food are both built from carbon, which is why one can be redirected from the bin towards the dinner plate.

Scientists already use living things as factories: the protein food Quorn has been made from a fungus and sold for decades, and in 2016 researchers in Japan discovered a bacterium, Ideonella sakaiensis, that naturally breaks PET down.
The idea of eating something that began as waste feels strange, but the science behind it — fermentation and single-cell protein — is old; what is new is applying it to plastic.

perspectives.description: Food scientists see a double win: edible protein made from plastic and farm waste could feed people in disaster zones or on long space missions while also cutting plastic pollution. The fact that a NASA competition backed the idea shows governments will fund unusual solutions.

Sceptics and food-safety campaigners worry about the unknowns. Growing food on plastic waste raises questions about leftover chemicals from the plastic, and the team itself is waiting for approval before any formal taste test — 'safe in the data so far' is not the same as approved.

Industry has used microbes as factories for decades — antibiotics, enzymes and even the protein Quorn come from fermentation. The genuinely new step here is the feedstock: PET, one of the hardest common plastics to break down, feeding an edible product rather than fuel or chemicals.

If approvals come through, the next hurdles are scale and trust. Can a 3D-printing system produce enough calories to matter, and will people eat a cookie that started life as a bottle? Disaster relief or space missions are likely to adopt it long before any supermarket shelf does.
